group.title: Town and transport
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: To travel regularly between your home and your place of work.
examples: I {commute} to the city by train every day.
wrong: He commutes to work, but he works from home and never leaves.

words.meaning: The busy time of day when many people go to or come home from work.
examples: The buses are packed during {rush hour}.
wrong: The roads are always empty at rush hour.

words.meaning: A long line of cars on a road that move very slowly or not at all.
examples: We were stuck in a {traffic jam} for an hour.
wrong: There was a traffic jam, so we drove quickly all the way.

words.meaning: A person walking in the street, not in a car.
examples: This street is only for {pedestrians}.
wrong: The pedestrian drove down the highway at high speed.

words.meaning: A marked place on a road where people can walk across safely.
examples: Cross the road at the {crosswalk}.
wrong: We parked our car in the middle of the crosswalk to sleep.

words.meaning: A place where two or more roads meet and cross.
examples: Turn left at the next {intersection}.
wrong: At the intersection the road had no other roads crossing it.

words.meaning: A circle where several roads meet and traffic goes around in one direction.
examples: Take the second exit at the {roundabout}.
wrong: The roundabout is a straight road with no turns at all.

words.meaning: One of the parts of a road, marked with lines, for a single line of cars.
examples: The bus moved into the left {lane}.
wrong: The highway had four lanes, all in one big strip with no lines.

words.meaning: The fastest speed you are allowed to drive on a road.
examples: The {speed limit} here is thirty miles an hour.
wrong: He kept to the speed limit by driving as fast as the car could go.

words.meaning: Money you pay to use a road or bridge.
examples: We paid a {toll} to cross the bridge.
wrong: The toll is money the bridge pays to every driver.

words.meaning: A longer way you take because the usual road is closed.
examples: The road was closed, so we took a {detour}.
wrong: We took a detour, the shortest and most direct way.

words.meaning: An area of homes on the edge of a city.
examples: They live in a quiet {suburb} and drive into town.
wrong: The suburb is in the very center of the city.

words.meaning: The outer parts of a town or city.
examples: The airport is on the {outskirts} of the city.
wrong: The outskirts of the city are right in the middle of downtown.

words.meaning: An area of a town or country with its own character.
examples: The theater {district} is busy at night.
wrong: A district is a single small house.

words.meaning: A wide street in a town, often with trees on both sides.
examples: The museum is on Fifth {Avenue}.
wrong: An avenue is a narrow path for one person in the forest.

words.meaning: A sign by a road that shows the way and how far it is to places.
examples: The {signpost} says the village is two miles away.
wrong: We followed the signpost, which gave no directions at all.

words.meaning: To travel by getting free rides from drivers you stop by the road.
examples: As students, we {hitchhiked} across Europe.
wrong: She hitchhiked by buying a train ticket.

words.meaning: A tire on a car or bike that has lost its air.
examples: I got a {flat tire} on the way to work.
wrong: My bike rode perfectly because of the flat tire.

words.meaning: A place where you buy fuel for your car.
examples: We stopped at a {gas station} to fill up.
wrong: We stopped at the gas station to see a doctor.

words.meaning: Something like gas or oil that is burned to make an engine work.
examples: The car ran out of {fuel} on the highway.
wrong: The car ran on no fuel at all, so it needed fuel every day.

words.meaning: To go past a slower car that is moving in the same direction.
examples: Don’t {overtake} on a bend.
wrong: He overtook the truck by staying behind it all the way.

words.meaning: To make the loud noise of a car horn.
examples: The taxi driver {honked} at the cyclist.
wrong: He honked the horn quietly so nobody heard a thing.

words.meaning: To make a car or bike slow down or stop.
examples: She {braked} hard when the cat ran into the road.
wrong: He braked to make the car go faster.

words.meaning: A strap in a car or plane that holds you in your seat.
examples: Always wear your {seatbelt} in the car.
wrong: I wore my seatbelt on my head like a hat.

words.meaning: The building where a city’s government works.
examples: You can get a parking permit at {city hall}.
wrong: City hall is a small shop that sells fruit.

words.meaning: A ticket that lets you ride the bus many times for a week, month or year.
examples: With a monthly {bus pass}, I travel as much as I like.
wrong: My bus pass only works for one trip on one day.

words.meaning: To get off one train and get on another to continue a journey.
examples: You have to {change trains} at the central station.
wrong: We changed trains by staying on the same train all the way.

words.meaning: A part of a road kept for people riding bicycles.
examples: I feel safer riding in the {bike lane}.
wrong: Cars must use the bike lane, not the road.

words.meaning: Walking, not using a car or bus.
examples: The beach is ten minutes away {on foot}.
wrong: We went on foot, so we took the bus.

words.meaning: Buses, trains and other vehicles that everyone can pay to use.
examples: The city has good {public transportation}, so I don’t need a car.
wrong: Public transportation is my own private car.

words.meaning: A machine where you buy tickets for a bus, train or parking.
examples: Buy your ticket at the {ticket machine} on the platform.
wrong: The ticket machine sells hot coffee and nothing else.

words.meaning: Describes an area where people live, not where there are shops or factories.
examples: It’s a quiet {residential} street with no stores.
wrong: The residential area is full of factories and nobody lives there.

words.meaning: A place where one car can be parked.
examples: It took twenty minutes to find a {parking space}.
wrong: The parking space was big enough for a pen.

words.meaning: A notice that tells you to pay money for parking in the wrong place.
examples: I got a {parking ticket} for stopping outside the bank.
wrong: The parking ticket was a gift for parking well.

words.meaning: To pull a car or boat behind another vehicle with a rope or chain.
examples: My car was {towed} away because I parked in the wrong place.
wrong: The truck towed the car by pushing it from in front.

words.meaning: A turn that takes a car back in the direction it came from.
examples: We missed the exit, so we made a {U-turn}.
wrong: He made a U-turn and kept going straight on.

words.meaning: A street that is closed at one end.
examples: The road is a {dead end}, so you have to turn back.
wrong: The street is a dead end, so it leads straight on to the next town.

words.meaning: To share a car with others to travel to the same place.
examples: Four of us {carpool} to work to save money.
wrong: We carpool to work, each driving our own car alone.

words.meaning: A place where taxis wait for passengers.
examples: There’s a {taxi stand} outside the station.
wrong: The taxi stand is where taxis are repaired.

words.meaning: A bus or train that makes short trips back and forth between two places.
examples: A free {shuttle} runs from the airport to the hotel.
wrong: The shuttle goes once a year on a long trip around the world.
